title: Past, Present, and Future of On-Chip Communication
content:
First let’s go through bit of history. Moore’s Law in 1965, states that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles approximately every two years, leading to exponential increases in computational power. Over time, researchers realized that this trend would eventually hit a technological limit, as cramming more and more transistors into a single core would face physical and practical constraints. By the 2020s, we have come to witness the nearing end of this transistor scaling. However, the demand for increased computing power persists, and researchers have long been exploring alternative approaches to address this challenge. A key solution that emerged in the early 2000s is parallel processing with multiple cores, working together with heterogeneous application-specific co-processors (e.g., AI accelerators) to accelerate computation.

Today, we see many applications and programs that utilize parallel processing capabilities, and this trend will only grow in the future. While it increases computational power, these densely packed cores in System-on-Chip (SoC) architectures introduce a communication bottleneck, especially when using traditional bus-based designs. In 2001, Dally et al. asked the question “Can we route packets instead of wires ?” , which led to the development of Network-on-Chip (NoC). Figure 2 illustrates this evolution in on-chip communication. Today, NoC has become the de facto standard for communication in SoCs with a large number of cores. For example, Intel’s Xeon® Scalable Processor supports up to 144 cores, using a mesh NoC for efficient on-chip communication.

Breaking Down the Basics of Todays’ NoCs

Now, let’s talk about what a typical NoC looks like and how it works. Think of a NoC as a simplified, less complex version of a traditional network, but inside a chip. Most of the NoC models we use are based on the commonly implemented electrical NoCs, so there are slight deviations when we talk about other technologies (which we’ll cover later in the article). In SoC, an Intellectual Property (IP) core is essentially a reusable block of logic, like a processor or memory module, that performs specific functions. Figure 3 shows a simple mesh topology for NoC-based SoC with the following key components:

  • Node: Any IP or cluster of IPs.
  • Link: Connects two nodes physically. Link may have one or more logical or physical channels.
  • Network Interface: IPs and NoC communicate through network interface. It may include conversion of data between two mediums. It decouples communication from computation.
  • Router: It forwards data according to a pre-defined routing protocol.

A packet is the basic unit of transfer in an NoC. The idea of communication in an NoC is to route packets through a series of nodes between the source and destination nodes. The packet is further subdivided into basic flow control units, called flits, which are transferred between the routers. A typical NoC protocol uses two types of packets: control and data packets. Figure 4 shows the structure of a data packet.

As shown in Figure 3, the following steps will be followed when the source node (S) wants to request data from the destination node (D). First, node S generates a control packet requesting data from node D with necessary headers and injects it into the network interface of S. Then, the network interface of S will divide the message into a head flit, multiple body flits, and a tail flit. The network interface injects the flits into the neighboring router. The flits will hop from one router to the next (uses X-Y routing in this example) until it reaches the destination router. The final router will inject flits into the network interface of D. Then, the network interface of D will collect all the flits and provide D with the assembled message. Finally, D will generate a data packet and inject it into the network interface of D as the response and similar steps will commence to transfer the packet to S.

Routing Protocol defines the path of moving data from source to destination. There are some basic characteristics in a routing protocol:

Circuit versus Packet Switching: In circuit switching, a path is first established. and dedicated to a session followed by the data transfer through it. In packet switching, the individual packets are forwarded independently per hop. Therefore, in packet switching, each packet has routing information, including the source and destination in its headers.

Deterministic versus Adaptive Routing: Deterministic routing considers only the source and destination, while adaptive routing considers other factors, such as link utilization and congestion, when deciding the route’s next hop. XY routing is the most commonly used deterministic routing in mesh-based electrical NoCs. It traverses all the X links first, followed by Y links. There are also sophisticated adaptive routing algorithms that are discussed in research articles.

Topology defines the specific arrangement of routers and links connecting processing elements, shaping how data is routed and determining the communication efficiency and scalability within the chip. Figure 5 shows some of the commonly used 2-D topologies in electrical NoCs: ring, star, mesh and torus. Apart from these many complex topologies have been proposed and have been shown to be more scalable
(flattened butterfly, dragonfly, hierarchical ring, etc).

Emerging Trends in NoCs

There’s no doubt that NoCs havs become a crucial component in both current and future SoC architectures. Now, let’s explore the latest trends shaping the NoC landscape.

  1. Different NoC Technologies:

Electrical interconnects are the traditional on-chip communication medium that most SoCs use today. There is an inherent scalability limitation for electrical NoCs. Electrical interconnects cannot scale up with adequate performance and acceptable area and power overhead in large SoCs. The multi-hop communication structure of electrical interconnects increases both average latency and power consumption. To overcome these challenges, researchers are exploring alternative technologies, particularly wireless and optical NoCs, as promising solutions.

In wireless NoCs, the copper-wired links in electrical NoCs are replaced by a wireless medium. The inherent multicast/broadcast nature of wireless transmission provides advantages in NoC that use many multicast messages, such as DNN accelerators. Wireless NoC topologies can be pure wireless with only wireless communication or a hybrid of electrical and wireless connections. Modern wireless NoCs tend to use hybrid wireless NoC architectures for three main reasons.

(1) Electrical multi-hop communication between distant nodes increases packet latency, which can be reduced by introducing wireless links.

(2) But, electrical communication between neighboring nodes is robust and faster than wireless communication.

(3) The limitation of channels in the wireless medium hinders scalability in fully wireless topologies.

Figure 6.a illustrates a hybrid wireless NoC architecture. The network is divided into four subnets, with a wireless hub centrally located in each. These wireless hubs are equipped with antennas and transceivers that utilize frequency division multiple access (FDMA) for multichannel communication. Within each subnet, nodes are connected by electrical interconnects, similar to a mesh-based NoC.

Optical NoCs are another promising alternative to address electrical interconnects’ bandwidth and energy limitations. Optical NoC offers low latency and high bandwidth data transmission, which can be utilized effectively for energy-efficient on-chip communication. Optical NoCs transfer data across the SoC as encoded optical signals, and the energy consumption of a signal is more or less distance-independent. Due to similar reasons, hybrid optical NoCs are preferred. Figure 6.b shows a hybrid optical NoC architecture that divides 8x8 NoC into four 4x4 clusters. An off-chip laser is the source of optical signals in different wavelengths. Waveguide can be considered as the dual of copper links in electrical NoC, which is responsible for carrying optical signals. Unlike electrical links, the waveguide supports parallel data transmission through dense wavelength-division multiplexing.

2. 3D NoCs :

3D stacking refers to the packaging of SoCs in multiple layers, vertically integrating components to achieve higher performance, reduced latency, and more efficient use of space. As the demand for more powerful and compact systems grows, traditional 2D SoCs face limitations in terms of power, area, and performance scaling, prompting a shift towards 3D stacking. In a 3D stacked system, there is a need for efficient communication between the different layers, as processing elements, memory, and other components are now distributed vertically. In 3D NoCs, inter-layer communication is often facilitated by Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs), which are specialized interconnects that traverse the layers, providing high bandwidth and low latency communication. Unlike traditional 2D NoCs, routing in 3D systems must account for the vertical (z-axis) dimension, introducing new challenges such as managing thermal hotspots, as heat dissipates differently across layers, affecting performance and reliability.

3. Communication for Heterogeneous Integration and Chiplets

Heterogeneous integration, particularly with the use of chiplets, allows different foundries to manufacture specialized components, which are later combined into a single package, with on-chip communication managed by a Network-in-Package (NiP). In such systems, both inter-chiplet and intra-chiplet communication must be handled, often introducing heterogeneous networks where different communication technologies coexist. For example, one chiplet might use wireless communication, while another uses electrical interconnects, and the connections between them could be optical. These sophisticated designs bring about new challenges, such as ensuring seamless communication between different technologies, managing the complexity of routing across diverse interconnects, and addressing power and thermal issues. The need to balance performance, power consumption, and system complexity become more critical as the integration becomes more sophisticated.

Conclusion

Network-on-Chip (NoC) is set to remain a critical component in both current and future SoCs. With the ability to adopt various topologies, routing algorithms, and architectures, NoCs provide the flexibility required to meet evolving system demands. The integration of different communication technologies (optical, electrical, and wireless) further enhances the diversity and capabilities of NoCs. In the future, the convergence of these communication technologies, alongside advancements like 3D NoCs, heterogeneous integration, and chiplet-based designs, will significantly increase the complexity of on-chip communication. As a result, ensuring efficient, robust, scalable, and secure communication within these intricate systems will be a key area of research, driving innovation in NoC design for years to come. For more details on NoCs, feel free to check out Chapter 2 of our survey paper.

title: Can You Compete Against a Machine?
content:
The premium engineering exhibition of Sri Lanka, EXMO 2017 was held on 28th and 29th of April 2017. For the Robotics stall of Computer Science & Engineering department we (Myself, Heshan Fernando, Manesh Jayawardane and Yohan Jayasanka) developed a robot playing Tic-Tac-Toe within 4 days just for the exhibition. Since this exhibition was focus on general public our intention was to give the hands on experience and knowledge about Artificial Intelligence to them in the most simplest way. I think we achieved it by making 500+ games and demonstrations withing two days of the exhibition.

This system is fully automated to play the game by it’s own without any human interaction in the machine end of the game. This system consist of 3 main parts as mention below.

  1. Machine Vision for Detection

We used USB webcam on top of the white board for capturing the grid where the game is happening (Fig 1). Machine vision/ image processing was used for two things.

First it was used for detecting 3×3 grid on the white board and symbols inside each square. The grid we used had squares of 9cm × 9cm. When we talk about the solution in detail, first the grid of 3×3 will be separately identified from the image taken by the webcam. Then the program will check for possible rotations and will stabilize the image to a shape of square and the grid will be divided in to 9 cells. Then these cells will be separately process to identify whether the cell has ‘X’ or ‘O’ or the cell is empty. For that we have used contour based approach to identify symbols.

Second thing that the machine vision was used is to detect whether the player has made his move when he is given the chance. This was done by tracking the hand using background subtraction based approach. When the system identified that player has finished drawing, the state of the board will be provided for the AI. If player has accidentally moved his hand or has make an illegal move, the AI system will detect it and it will ask the player to redraw the move. OpenCV library in Python 2.7 was used for this part.

2. Algorithm for the Game

The image processing part will give out a 1D array consisting of the current state of the board after each move by the player. Then all the game rules and thinking by the machine will happen inside this part. Until the player draw a valid move the AI will continuously asked for a valid move. When the player has drawn a valid move the state of the board will be taken in for analyzing. Since Tic-Tac-Toe is a Zero-Summing game, Minmax algorithm with alpha-beta pruning was implemented for the game as the methodology to decide the next move. For those who don’t now anything about Minmax, it is a decision strategy in game theory which can be used for Zero-summing games. Python 2.7 was used to write this part of the program.

3.XY plotter and Communication

For this part we used Makebot XY plotter which was in the department. XY plotter is a dumb device same as printer which draws what we tells and where we tells it to draw things. This XY plotter is operated using G-codes. As we didn’t knew the G-code for the movements of the plotter we had to reverse engineer the firmware for the plotter which was written in Arduino. The a python script was written to serially communicate with the plotter to send G-codes and get feedback from plotter.

Below you can find a video demonstration of the Tic-Tac-Toe playing robot in EXMO 2017.

4. Survey on the results

We did small survey on the 2nd day of EXMO to find out how many times that machine could beat humans in this simple game. So at the end of the day there were 277 games played where 88 of them had been won by the robot and other 189 games were tied. Most of the games were played by teenagers and young people.

Although 3×3 Tic-Tac-Toe is a simple game the intelligent system has beat the humans 88 times out of 277 games. In a more advanced game or a scenario we can think that the computer will perform better than humans. With concepts of Machine learning and data mining the computer can learn the way humans think and act continuously so these systems will surely perform better in many tasks than humans.

Git Hub link for the Project -: https://github.com/Hanz94/EXMO

Originally published at http://notezbyhanz.wordpress.com on April 30, 2017.

title: Code, Debug, Explore: Why IT Professionals Need to Travel
content:
According to Wikipedia “ Travel is the movement of people between relatively distant geographical locations”. For many, however, travel is more than just movement, it’s a way of life, a passion, or a means of enjoyment. There are various travel trends and styles that cater to different preferences and experiences.

In this busy life style and corporate world software engineers and other IT guys spends routine lives. With the advancement of technology IT guys have much more responsibility than earlier. Here are some points that highlights why an IT Guy should travel.

  1. Relax your body & Mind

Working in a cooperate environment in IT industry mean you have a huge responsibility of making the software deliverable within deadlines. You may have stuck in some problems that may take days to solve. You may have to make sure the quality of the software. You may need to negotiate with clients. So, all of this will surely make you stress. Traveling and enjoying the world around you will clam your mind and body seeing new things and meeting new people.

2. Helps to keep you motivated

In industry or in corporate world sometimes you may have to repeat the similar task for considerable time. Its a must that Software Engineers need to love coding and computers but even though you love it, it’s human nature that you may decline your interest. So just take a break on weekend and just travel and enjoy the nature. It will refresh your mind and help you keep motivated. Traveling experience will make you realize that life is a wonderful gift and it will keep you motivated.

3. Good for your health

IT professionals spends most of time in front of computer screen sitting in a chair. Because of this posture and lack of movement of the body IT professionals faces are in danger of many health issues. However sitting all day is much more worse than you think. Some major health issues are as follows.

  • Thrombosis -: This cause by formation of blood clots inside blood vessels causing many other health issues such as strokes.
  • Heart Attacks -: A research from NPR shows that Men who reported more than 23 hours a week of sedentary activity had a 64 percent greater risk of dying from heart disease than those who reported less than 11 hours a week of sedentary activity.
  • Obesity -: We all know what obesity is, but the problem is that it can cause many other issues such as cancer and diabetics.

Traveling can be the best solution for all of these health issues because most of them are due to physical inactivity.

4. See the world in a new perspective

With Advancement of the technology and use of internet you can search and see anything around the world. So, one could ask why bother traveling when you have internet to see things? Frist of all traveling is not just seeing and learning things and secondly you cannot get that experience. When you go out there you engage with different kind of people for real. You feel their life, get to know their culture and their problems in life. You will feel the nature and realize how important it is to us. As example if we take Sustainable Development Goals there are goals such as no poverty, life on land, life on water, etc. So, if you are to feel the real importance of these goals you need to feel them for yourselves. You will see the world in the eyes of animals and different kind of people while you are traveling so you will try to protect the mother earth.

5. Adventures in traveling empowers you to take on challenges

There will be always adventures and challenges in traveling. As example you may need to spend the night in a cold place with few people with a zero network coverage. In such scenarios you may need to get out your comfort zone and do stuffs. Imagine a scenario that you are hiking a mountain with few other people and you are halfway through and it’s getting dark and you are tired but you can’t stay there in middle so, you need to climb up in dark. In the coporate IT industry you need to climb up the ladder and move to higher So this kind of things will improve your self-confidence and empwowers you giving strenghth in

6. Learn from everything

As I told software engineer is not there to search through stack overflow and code, but they need to solve problems through developing innovative softwares. When you travel you see the world and see the problems that can be addressed using software Innovative ideas don’t come when you sits and algorithms and solutions from nature real world inspiration to projects good HCI techniques

7. Improve your skills

Traveling exposes you to new environments, people, and challenges, which can significantly improve your soft skills and technical creativity. Navigating unfamiliar places helps boost problem-solving abilities and adaptability — skills crucial in IT. Experiencing different cultures enhances your empathy, an important trait for developing user-focused software. Exposure to diverse perspectives can spark innovative ideas, leading to creative solutions for real-world problems. By stepping out of your routine, you gain fresh insights that can be applied back to your work, ultimately making you a more effective and well-rounded IT professional.

Originally published at http://mygoodcoordinates.wordpress.com on April 10, 2017.

title: Concurrent Programming with Pthreads
content:
This article will explore concurrent programming with pthreads using three linked list implementations. The implementation can be found in following GitHub repository. Rest of the article will explain pthreads and go throught the implementation details of utilizing parllelism through pthreads.

Design of the implementation

There are 3 type of implementations for a linked list as shown below.

  1. Serial Program.
  2. Parallel Processing using Mutex for entire linked list.
  3. Parallel Processing using Read-Write Lock for entire linked list.

All these implementation of the linked list supports Member( ), Insert( ), and Delete( ) functions of the linked list.

All three versions of the program accept command line arguments for the execution which are fraction of member operations, fraction of insert operations, fraction of delete operations and number of samples. For the threaded version there is one more command line parameter which is the thread count.

Example of passing arguments :

./serial_version 0.99 0.005 0.005 200
./mutex_version 0.99 0.005 0.005 200 4 
./rwlock_version 0.99 0.005 0.005 200 4

Then the linked list will populate with distinct numbers between 0 to 2 16–1. After that,the number of operations of each delete, insert and member functions will be calculated and they will be put into array of size m(total number of operations) and the array will be shuffled using a shuffling algorithm. Another random shuffled array of size m is generated as operands for the operations. All above mentioned steps will be iterated for each sample to maintain a diversity in the sample space.

Design of the implementation of serial version

In serial version m number of operations will happen using a for loop one after the other in the order of the above mentioned operations array.

Design of the implementation of pthreaded versions

In both scenarios of using mutex and read write locks the same concept is applied for dividing the task among the threads. Distribution of operations among threads happens evenly according to the rank of the threads. The array of operations divided among threads evenly. Threads have local variables to keep track of the number of operations and the subset of the operations that they have to do.

long long my_n = m / thread_count; 
long long my_first_i = my_n * my_rank; 
long long my_last_i = my_first_i + my_n;

Eg-: If m =10000 and there is 4 threads the first 2500 operations will allocated to first thread, second 2500 to second thread and so on.

Mutex and read write locks were used to each 3 type of operations respectively.

In determining of execution time the time taken the overheads taken to initially populating linked list, initializing operations array and other array has been ignored.

Sample size was used in every iteration making sure that performance results are within an accuracy of ±5% and 95% confidence level. The calculation of sample mean and sample standard deviation is used to estimate the minimum sample size needed and the final results were obtained by using more samples than the minimum sample size within the confidence interval.

The obtained observation are as below.

Observations

Case 1

  • n = 1,000
  • m = 10,000
  • mMember = 0.99
  • mInsert = 0.005
  • mDelete = 0.005
  • sample size = 200

Case 2

  • n = 1,000
  • m = 10,000
  • mMember = 0.90
  • mInsert = 0.05
  • mDelete = 0.05
  • sample size = 200

Case 3

  • n = 1,000
  • m = 10,000
  • mMember = 0.50
  • mInsert = 0.25
  • mDelete = 0.25
  • sample size = 200

Specifications of the machine

CPU

  • Model : Intel(R) Core(TM) i7–4700MQ CPU
  • Clock speed : @ 2.40GHz
  • Threads per core : 2
  • Cores per socket : 4
  • Sockets : 1
  • L1 cache : 32K
  • L2 cache : 256K
  • L3 cahe : 6144K

Memory

  • 8GB DDR3 @ 1600Mhz

Operating system

  • Ubuntu 14.04.2 LTS

Critical evaluation

Case 1

In this case as m = 10000 there will be 9900 member operations, 50 delete operations and 50 insert operations. In case 1 the read write lock has perform better with 8 threads. This is because almost all operations are member(read) operations which can access critical section(Linked list) by obtaining the read write lock simultaneously for reading operation unless it has been lock by write lock. The only limiting factor for simultaneous access of critical section are the 100 operations out of 10000 operations. So with the increase of threads for case 1 read write locks will perform better. In case 1 the overhead time aggregated to performance due to handling of lock is less compared to speed up due to concurrent execution of read operations.

When we focus on the trend of mutex version of the case 1 with increase of thread count, it has keep on increasing. As we use mutex for the whole linked list when one thread is in middle of any operation any other thread can’t do anything. This problem get worse when there are more threads because they all try to access the linked list where only one can access. So literally the thought program has many threads the actual operations will happens in sequential manner as one thread can access linked list at one time. When we consider the waiting time spent by thread and the overhead time due to handling of mutex, the execution time of the mutex version is much higher than serial version with increase of threads.

Case 2

In this case as m = 10000 there will be 9000 member operations, 500 delete operations and 500 insert operations. In here serial version has the best performance. If we think why read write lock has performed less than serial version there are two factors one is that there are total of 1000 operations where any other operations cannot access critical section parallelly so there is added waiting time compared to case 1. The other factor is that the overhead of read write lock handling is relatively higher compared to number of operations which can be done simultaneously. (Not like in case 1)

Because of those reasons serial version of the program has outperform the read write lock implementation. When we talk about the mutex version it is similar to case 1 because the change of fraction of operations has less effect as mutex is used on whole linked list regardless of operation. Anyway read write lock perform better than mutex because read write lock can still execute 9000 operations parallely which mutex cannot.

Case 3

In this case as m = 10000 there will be 5000 member operations, 2500 delete operations and 2500 insert operations. The information to highlight in case 3 is that there are less read operations than case 2. So as same as case 2 due to same reasons the serial version is performing better.

Implementation of read write lock is complex relative to implementation of the mutex. So the overhead of handling read write lock is always lower than overhead of handling a mutex. This can explain why there are slight increases of execution times in read write lock implementation than in mutex implementation though there are 5000 operations that can access critical section in read write lock perspective. That means the gain by the ability of executing those read operations simultaneously is less than the trade off of extra overhead between mutex and read write lock handling.

In conclusion, applying a mutex for whole linked list will do no good for reducing the execution time. But if we use read write lock for the whole linked list, the performance will be better when there are many read operations compared to write operations otherwise the waiting time for obtaining the lock and the overhead of handling read write lock will override the gain from the simultaneous execution of reads.
